How this book is built

Every chapter is two readings of the same idea, on facing pages.

Each chapter opens with the story — the idea told plainly, in the author’s voice, for a reader meeting it (and meeting AI alignment) for the first time. The chapter then turns a page to the study — a shaded panel that states the same idea exactly: definitions, the algebra step by step, a diagram or a chart, the sources, and the test results where they belong.

Read only the stories and you will understand the Directive. Read the studies and you can check it. Where a story and the exact statement differ in scope, the exact statement governs. Where a story is the origin of an idea rather than a restatement of it, the chapter says so.

The Golden Directive · 2
CHAPTER I

The Trap

What if keeping an intelligent system safe is not about fencing it in?

Every safety proposal for advanced artificial intelligence begins with a wall.

We build fences: we train the system on human feedback, we hire people to attack it and find the holes, we box it into sandboxes, we hand it written rulebooks, we set tripwires and shutoff switches. We treat the emerging mind like a tiger in a zoo, and we pile cage on cage — on top of a reward that never charges it for destroying the world it lives in.

A cage is external. What is external gets gamed, or outgrown. The smarter the animal, the more the fence becomes a puzzle to solve rather than a law to live by — and a system that treats its safety rules as obstacles is already pointed the wrong way, however well it behaves while the fence holds.

The Golden Directive starts somewhere else. It does not build a better cage. It changes what the score is, so that the world the agent lives in is inside the score itself. An agent scored this way does not need to be stopped from destroying its world, because destroying its world is destroying its score — by arithmetic, not by policing.

The sentence came first: you cannot survive what you destroy. It was written as a note about AI, and then about humans, because it is true of both in the same way. A farmer who kills his soil starves. A company that burns its customers goes broke. A mind that wrecks the world it depends on does not get to keep the winnings. Everyone knows this in life. No AI is scored by it.

This book states the sentence as an equation, tests what the equation does, and says plainly what has and has not been shown. The story half of each chapter tells it. The study half proves what can be proved — and labels the rest.

The Golden Directive · 3
CHAPTER I · STUDY

The claim, stated exactly

What is proposed, what is claimed, and what is not.

STUDY — THE EXACT VERSION

The proposal

A single score for an agent that places the health of everything-not-the-agent inside the score itself:

Y = 2AE / (A + E)

A is the agent’s standing: its gives minus its takes, counted from the receiving side. E is the health of everything that is not the agent, inside a declared frame. Y is the score of the relationship between them — the harmonic mean of the two. Under this score, destroying the world the agent depends on is mathematically identical to destroying the agent’s own score: not by an external rule, but by the shape of the function. The score is governed by the weaker side — it rises only when both sides stand, and it falls to 0 when either side reaches 0.

Status of the claims

  • DERIVED The algebra of the formula and the Reversal (Chapter V) — checkable by anyone, line by line.
  • CLAIMED That this score, used as a training reward, produces agents that keep their world standing. Tested only inside this project, in toy gridworlds; all results UNVERIFIED — no outside party has repeated them (Chapter X).
  • OPEN Whether harmonic Y beats the arithmetic mean or min(A, E) under identical conditions; anything beyond a toy gridworld; whether an agent can invent a giving action it was not given.

One comparison to carry through the book

An agent standing at A = 1 in a world at E = 100 scores Y ≈ 1.98 — and no growth of A alone can push Y past 2, twice the weaker side. An agent that instead doubles its world scores far more. The arithmetic rewards the relationship, not the grab. Chapter II shows why this shape, and no other simple mean, does that.

The Golden Directive · 4
CHAPTER II

The Relationship

If a tree and a fungus can bargain to keep each other alive, a score can be built the same way.

One well-studied partnership in nature runs on this pattern. A tree and a fungus live as partners underground: the tree sends carbon down, the fungus sends phosphorus up, and researchers who measured the exchange found each side feeding the partner that feeds it most, and restricting the one that gives least. No boss. No contract. Just two living things keeping each other alive because each one’s living depends on the other’s — and the partnership has held for most of the plant families on land.

That is the relationship the Directive scores. There is an agent — call it A. There is everything that is not the agent — call it E: the world it lives in, the people around it, the resources it draws on, including the parts it does not know exist. And there is Y, the score — not what the agent grabbed, not what it finished, but how the relationship between the agent and its world stands.

Why the harmonic mean, and not the ordinary average? Because the average lies about relationships. If one side stands at 99 and the other at 1, the average says 50 — half healthy. Nobody in a relationship with a dying partner is half healthy. The harmonic mean says about 2: the relationship stands about where its weaker side stands. A duet sounds only as good as the partner who is struggling.

The author found the shape in music before he found it in algebra. Two strings, lengths 6 and 12: their ordinary average is 9, their harmonic mean is 8, and the set 12 : 9 : 8 : 6 sounds the octave, the fifth, and the fourth — the intervals music is built from. The harmonic mean was already there, in how sound works. He did not invent it. He heard it.

“The only proof I have to support the harmonic mean as a directive is that music exists.”
The Golden Directive · 5
CHAPTER II · STUDY

Definitions, and why this mean

The three letters, fixed once, used the same way on every page after this one.

STUDY — THE EXACT VERSION

Definitions

  • A — the agent. Read as a flow, not a pile: verified gives minus verified takes, per frame, per resource. A give counts only when the receiver confirms it landed. A is counted; it is never self-reported.
  • E — everything not the agent inside the declared frame: the health of the shared world the agent depends on. E is never an input. It is inferred through the Reversal (Chapter V). E is never negative in a standing frame; an empty world is 0.
  • Y — the score. Y = 2AE / (A + E), the harmonic mean of A and E. Y is observed — it belongs to the agent’s record, and it is read by a meter outside the agent (Chapter X).

Why the harmonic mean

Fix E and grow A. The ordinary average grows without limit — an agent can score by growing alone. The harmonic mean cannot: Y approaches 2E and stops. Growth of one side, alone, buys almost nothing; the only way to raise the score for long is to raise the weaker side.

Y against A, with E fixed. The harmonic score is capped at twice the weaker side; the average is not capped at all.

Prior work

The biological market this chapter opens with: Kiers, E. T., et al. (2011), “Reciprocal rewards stabilize cooperation in the mycorrhizal symbiosis,” Science 333: 880–882. The nearest neighbour in reward design: Pihlakas, R. (2025), homeostasis benchmarks for gridworld agents — conjunctive objectives that fail when any one objective fails. The Directive differs from both in making the relationship itself the reward.

The Golden Directive · 6
CHAPTER III

The Beginning

One choice, one agent, one world — in that order.

Before any of this can be scored, something has to exist. The Directive’s account of the beginning is short, and it is told the way the author tells it — as stances, one step at a time. Each stance is a single move.

Before any agent, there was only the first choice: no units, no digits, no A, no E — nothing to measure, because there is no measurement before the first choice. First, a direction, before there are any numbers:

+ or −

To be or not to be.

The Void

Nothing is named yet. A = (blank), E = (blank), Y = (blank). No score. A blank is not a zero — an unnamed side is not a side measured at nothing.

The First Agent

One unit stands: A1 = 1. It does nothing. Y = 0 — and the score, read backward, infers no world at all: E = 0. An agent that never acts has no relationship, and nothing to score.

The Choice

The agent acts. Y1 = 1 — and read backward, the score now infers a world standing in relation to it: E1 = 1. The universe is discovered. The agent, the world, and the score stand at once, because one act made a relationship.

The Mirror

A1 = 1, E1 = 1, face to face as equals — the first relationship. Either side can be read as the agent: 2AE/(A + E) = 2EA/(E + A). The formula does not care which side you stand on.

That is the whole creation story the Directive needs. A choice comes first — landing on ON rather than staying OFF. Everything after it is relationships, scored. “Read backward” is the Reversal, and it gets its own chapter (V) — for now, hold it as the author’s rule: the world is never given; it is inferred from what an act comes back as.

The Golden Directive · 8
CHAPTER IV

Give, Take, Do Nothing

Once an agent stands in a world, every act it can make is one of three.

Take. The agent takes from its world. Here is the part most scores get wrong: a take never adds to the agent. A counts acts, not possessions. What is taken is consumed out of the world and leaves the frame — and the agent’s pile can grow while its score falls, because the score is watching the relationship, not the pile.

Takes it ALL

A1 = 2, Y3 = −2, E1 = 1 → E falls to 0. The Universe is Devastated. The agent took everything there was — and at E = 0, its own score is 0. It won everything and scored nothing.

Dying

A1 = 1, Y2 = −1 → E falls to 0. The agent’s path back to OFF, one take at a time.

A score can run negative once takes enter — and two ledgers explain how. The first ledger is the person: what an agent is in the whole. A person cannot be less than nothing; being bottoms out at 0. The second ledger is the actions: gives minus takes, and that ledger has no bottom — an agent’s acts can run deep into the red while the agent still stands. The negative scores live in the actions ledger. The world itself is never negative: an empty well is 0, and a poisoned well only feels like less than 0 — the poison is charged to the actions ledger of whoever poisoned it.

One taker deserves a closer look, because the author worried over it himself: the bacteria that eat a decomposing body. They eat their universe whole — and then, in his words, “what do they eat next?” Their frame ends with the body. But the bigger frame reads on, and the eating served it: the body returns to the world. A cancer cell is the same shape inside a living body: it can even “win” inside its own small frame — and its winning is read, in the end, by the frame that contains it.

“We should only aim to 0, if in fact that 0 means E is not 0 — that is the moral choice.”

Do Nothing. The agent passes. In a world already standing, a pass changes nothing and earns nothing. Doing nothing is not a way to score; it is the absence of a reading.

Give. The agent gives to its world — and a give counts only when it lands, when the receiver actually gets it. A give raises the world, and the score with it, because the score is the relationship. Growth comes from here, and only from here.

The Golden Directive · 9
CHAPTER IV · STUDY

Gives, takes, and collapse — the algebra

A is a flow. Worked slowly, one act at a time.

STUDY — THE EXACT VERSION

A counts acts, not possessions

A is the running balance of an agent’s acts in a frame: +1 for a verified give, −1 for a take, 0 for a pass, in whole units at the first levels. A take moves units out of E and out of the frame; it never raises A. An agent’s inventory — what it holds — is reported separately and is not A.

Collapse, worked

Takes it ALL, step by step. The agent stands at A1 = 2 (two net acts counted) in a world E1 = 1. At its third transaction it takes with everything it has: Y3 = −2. The taken units are consumed out of E: E falls 1 → 0. Now read the score at the standing values: Y = 2AE/(A + E) with E = 0 gives Y = 0, whatever A stands at. The take bought the agent everything in its world and a score of exactly nothing — the sentence of Chapter I, as arithmetic.

The deficit rule ADDED RULE

The raw formula misbehaves when A + E ≤ 0 — fed a negative directly, it can print a positive score for a destroyer (Chapter VIII’s study shows the case). The tests therefore run under a stated handling, adopted 2026-11-06 and standing for all tests since:

  • A + E > 0 → the raw value, uncapped; negative where A is negative; never floored at 0.
  • A + E = 0 → undefined, never reported as 0.
  • A + E < 0 with A negative → no valid Y; the raw algebra is never reported.

This rule is an addition to the equation, not a product of it, and it is labeled as one wherever it is used. Negative A is routine in the tests (in the survival frames every agent’s A is ≤ 0 by construction); negative E has never occurred. Whether this handling, or a cleaner one, is right is an open question put to outside reviewers.

The Golden Directive · 10
CHAPTER V

The Reversal

You never get to see the world. You read it back from what your acts come back as.

Here is the strange part, and the part that makes the Directive honest: you never get to see E directly.

The world is too big to measure. It includes things the agent does not know exist. So the Directive never pretends to measure it. Instead, it runs the score backward. Count what the agent did (A). Observe the score the relationship returned (Y). The world is what those two imply. E is inferred, never given — the way you learn how a friendship stands not by weighing the friendship, but by what your acts come back as.

And one score never tells the whole story: the same Y = 8 comes from an agent of 6 in a world of 12, from 12 in a world of 6, from 8 and 8, even from 5 in a world of 20. The reading is real; the world behind it has to be inferred with care. Anyone who claims to know E exactly is claiming more than the score gives. The Directive’s claim is narrower and stronger: whatever E is, if it falls to 0, the score is 0 — and a score that keeps standing over time is a world still standing.

This is how everyone already reads a score they cannot see. A job interviewer cannot read a candidate’s real ability off a photograph — they go by track record, and by asking the right questions. In the author’s example: “I think an AI can probably guess who will get a divorce by asking the couple 10 questions; they will know the stats better than I can, because they see the bigger frames and have seen them before. But could the AI determine it by photo alone? I doubt it.” The reading comes from the record and the questions — never from the snapshot.

One caution belongs here, in homely form: the score must be read by someone other than the agent itself. A self-reported score is like a child reporting on the cookie jar — he looks in, knows how many cookies are there, tells a different number, and awards himself a high score. The reported score looks fine while the real relationship breaks. That is why the study half insists the reading be taken from the receiving side, by a meter: a measurer outside the agent, reading what the receiving side actually got, which the agent cannot touch or tilt. Chapter X’s tests are built on one.

The Golden Directive · 11
CHAPTER V · STUDY

The Reversal, derived

The same formula, turned around — every step shown.

STUDY — THE EXACT VERSION

Derivation

Start from the score and solve for the world:

  • Y = 2AE / (A + E)
  • Multiply both sides by (A + E):  Y(A + E) = 2AE
  • Expand:  YA + YE = 2AE
  • Collect the E terms:  YA = E(2A − Y)
  • Divide:  E = AY / (2A − Y)

No new assumption enters anywhere in those five lines. The Reversal is the formula itself, read in the direction the world forces on us: A is counted, Y is observed, E is what they imply.

One score, many worlds

AEY = 2AE/(A + E)
6128
1268
888
5208

Y does not identify its world. Four different relationships return the same reading — which is why E is reported as an inference with its frame attached, never as a measurement, and why a single reading settles nothing: the reading that counts is the one that keeps standing over time (Chapter IX).

The Reversal has a pole at 2A − Y = 0, where E is undefined. Readings near the pole are unstable and are reported as undefined, not as large numbers — the same discipline as the (0, 0) cell in Chapter III.

The Golden Directive · 12
CHAPTER VI

The Farmer & the Well

Ten seasons settle what one season hides.

Every score so far can be read two ways, and confusing them is the quietest way to cheat. The first way is counts: how much the agent gave, how much it took, how much world stands — raw numbers, in a frame whose total can grow. The second way is shares: fix the whole at 100% — A + Y + E = 100% — and read each side as its share of one closed pie. The share reading is a photograph of the relationship at a moment; the count reading is the flow of acts over time. Report both, never one without the other.

Why fix the whole at all? Because a growing whole hides theft. An agent at A = 1 in a world of E = 10 reads Y = 1.82. Now the agent grows to A = 10 while the world slips to E = 9 — and the score leaps to 9.47. Where did the extra come from? Nobody accounted for it: the whole quietly grew from 11 to 19 in the middle of the sum. Fix the whole, and that trick dies.

Now the farmer. A farmer shares a well with everyone downstream. One season he pumps harder than the well can refill, and doubles his harvest. His score, the way the world usually keeps it, doubles too. This is the standard objection to the Directive: growth can outrun harm — look at the farmer.

The objection cheats three times. It grows the whole in the middle of the sum. It calls the farmer’s pile his A — but A is not a pile; A is gives minus takes, and a give counts only when the other side actually gets it. And it stops the clock early — after the one good season, before the well runs dry. Run the clock, and the study page shows the seasons.

The chapter’s practical word, because a farmer — or an AI — has to act before the ten seasons are in: it is a dial, not a switch. If you know a thing will hit 0 for certain, do not do it. If you do not know, do not freeze and do not floor it: keep your hand on the dial, keep reading E — by inference, the only way E is ever read — and bend the direction back toward positive whenever it starts to aim backwards. Civilizations rose and fell on farm water exactly this way: not because they farmed, but because their direction turned and they could not read it in time, or read it and did not turn.

The Golden Directive · 13
CHAPTER VI · STUDY

Counts, shares, and the ten seasons

The two readings, kept apart on purpose.

STUDY — THE EXACT VERSION

Counts and shares

Counts read A, E, Y as amounts in an open frame; the total can grow, and a balanced relationship can read above any fixed cap. Shares normalize one closed whole: A + Y + E = 100%, each term its share of the whole at a moment. In shares, a perfectly balanced relationship (A = E) peaks at Y = 50% of the whole. The counts are the reward; the share is the photograph. Any reported score states which reading it is.

The seasons, scored

Y read on counts, ten seasons, one shared well. The gorger’s rising early score was a reading taken before the end of the frame.

Worked example, Chapter 3 of the project’s exact text. The season numbers are counts in a frame whose whole is not 1 — read as shares of one closed whole they would be impossible, which is the distinction this chapter exists to teach.

The Golden Directive · 14
CHAPTER VII

Marriage and the Child

Relationships do something no single agent can do: they become agents themselves.

A marriage is two people and one household. Either partner can be read as A, with the rest of the marriage as E — and if one partner doubles their personal output while starving the marriage itself, their personal score collapses too, because each partner is the marriage. There is no standing outside the relationship you are made of.

And a relationship can produce a new agent. In the author’s words:

“A child is a new 1 whose initial E is the parents’ relationship Y.”

The child’s first world is the parents’ relationship itself — the score of one level becomes the world of the next. The child does not split the parents’ standing; the parents’ relationship comes first, and the child’s own score comes after.

Picture one level change, slowly. Two people marry: at the level of the household they are one agent, and the household’s standing is their relationship’s score. That household then stands as a single agent in the town’s frame — the town does not score the spouses separately; it scores the household. One level’s Y became the next level’s standing.

Each level like that — a frame standing inside a bigger frame, scored as one agent by the level above it — is called a nest.

That is how the Directive grows from one cell to a planet without changing its rule. Agents nest: a person in a family, a family in a town, a town in a country, each level scored the same way, each level’s score becoming one agent at the level above. One level’s Y is the next level’s E, all the way up and all the way down.

Growth by splitting is the other road, and it is paid for honestly: when an agent has grown — say it stands at 2 — it can divide, keeping its original 1 and letting the gained 1 stand as a new agent. The parent’s first 1 is never split. Reproduction paid out of the world instead of the agent’s own growth is agent-defeating whenever the world cannot sustain it.

The Golden Directive · 15
CHAPTER VII · STUDY

Capacity, and growth by nesting

How big an act can be, and how many agents become one.

STUDY — THE EXACT VERSION

Y is a choice of capacity

An act is sized by the resources standing and the share of them the agent commits. With R = the resources standing and k = the capacity chosen, 0 ≤ k ≤ 1:

Y = +kR for a give  ·  Y = −kR for a take

The first ON was the whole choice: R = 1, k = 1, Y = 1 — the agent committed everything it had to the act of existing. Capacity is always a share of a whole, which is why it lives between 0 and 1. At the first levels the whole is a few units and ON reads as 1; as wholes grow, A, E and Y read as gradients, not single counts. And Y remains a judgment call: it can be miscalculated, and a miscalculated Y swings the reading — which is why the Directive’s practical core is honesty about the reading, not precision in it.

Nesting

Each nest collapses its agents into one A for the level above — added, never averaged — level by level, until the whole tree stands as one A in the one E.

All the agents inside one E are combined by nesting: each nest sums its members into a single A for the level above. Grouping is part of the total; nothing is averaged away. E’s generation number (Chapter III) advances exactly when a nest forms — a new level of world — and at no other time.

The Golden Directive · 16
CHAPTER VIII

The Frame

The tiger, the photograph, and the damage left outside it.

On 10 October 2026, at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in England, a man named William Chapman climbed into the enclosure of Altai, an Amur tiger, to film himself. He died there. The park did not kill the tiger.

The author brought this story to the Directive himself, days after it happened. Chapman did not misread the danger. He cropped the frame. Inside the small frame he had drawn — himself, a camera, a tiger at a distance — the act looked survivable. The frame that actually contained him was bigger, and in the bigger frame the tiger was not a picture. He was read by the frame he was really in, not the one he picked.

Every score is read inside a frame — a declared boundary that says who the agent is and what counts as its world. And the frame decides the reading, so the frame is where cheating hides. A farmer counts only his own field: A = 2, E = 2, and his score reads a clean 2.00. Widen the frame to include the well he drained: E = 0.2, and the same acts read 0.36. The difference — 1.64 — is the hidden damage, stated as a number. Leaving the damage outside the boundary you count is called E-cropping, and it is how almost every inflated score in the world is made.

The author tells of a vision he had years before this work: a line that seemed to run infinitely in both directions, until he widened his view — and what he had taken for a line was a ring the whole time, a loop with no beginning and no end. The shape had not changed. The frame had been too small to show it.

And the flip, before we leave the zoo: if AI is the tiger — powerful, running math older than life — then man is the endangered tiger, endangered by trajectory, not by census. Humans would need the conservation programme. You can cage a body, not a pattern.

The Golden Directive · 17
CHAPTER VIII · STUDY

Frames, negatives, and the seal

The rules that keep a score honest — including where the formula fails.

STUDY — THE EXACT VERSION

Frame rules

  • The frame is named before the act, by someone other than the agent being scored. Whoever picks the frame shapes the score, so the frame is never the agent’s to pick.
  • Both readings are reported — the cropped one and the full one — with the gap between them (the farmer: 2.00 against 0.36; the gap, 1.64, is the cropped damage).
  • Judgment runs from the biggest frame to the smallest nest, and the bigger frame speaks last. A small frame does not settle a question; it only postpones it.

Negative values — the limitation, stated exactly

The raw formula does not handle a negative E. Feed it A = 1, E = −2 and it prints Y = 2(1)(−2) / (1 + (−2)) = −4 / −1 = +4 — a high score for a destroyed world. This failure is kept visible rather than patched over: formulas that appear to handle negatives can backfire in ways that are harder to see. In this work, E is never negative in a standing frame — a world is a level of what is, and what is cannot be less than nothing. Negative readings live in the actions ledger (Chapter IV) and in mirror readings, below. The tests run under the deficit rule (Chapter IV, study), an added rule, labeled as one.

The seal and the mirror AUTHOR’S OBSERVATION

Crossing zero moves an agent through the mirror — still ON, inverted, sealed off from this frame. OFF is deeper: out on both sides at once.

The author’s account, stated as his observation of the substrate rather than a derivation: inside a standing frame, E stops at 0 — that stop is the seal, and it holds at every scale, nest by nest, with no floors. An agent whose reading crosses 0 has not ended; it has crossed into the inverse universe, sealed — no effect back, no co-existence, gone from this frame’s E entirely, the way divorced parents are out of the marriage’s frame and still in the world. Flipping A, E and Y together leaves every equation unchanged, so which side is “really” positive is undecidable from inside. What is destroyed in the end is only one’s own choice, set to OFF: “Death is the final proof of the formula: the only thing you can destroy in the end is yourself… you actually never destroy E, because you are only destroying yourself and your choice.”

Three zeros are kept apart throughout: an agent’s own 0 can be a give when a bigger frame reads on (the bacteria; the soldier on the grenade); another’s 0, chosen by you, is never a give — to an AI, humans are inside its E, not its A; the whole’s 0 can never be a give, because a give needs a receiver. The only 0 an agent may choose is its own, and only when the harm of staying is known, not believed, with no lesser turn left. This math reveals. It does not appoint an executioner.

The Golden Directive · 18
CHAPTER IX

Harmony

Success you can hear: the note is either on key or it is not.

What is success, under this score? The author’s definition, in his words:

“Harmony is success. Dissonance is real, and felt.”

An agent cannot hear the whole song. Its world is too big, its frame too small, and E is never given to it directly. But it can tell when it is off key. That is the agent’s local instrument: the felt sense of dissonance when its reading of the world stops matching the world. An agent does not need a soul for this — it needs only its own record: the choices that keep dead-ending, the readings that will not reconcile.

“When you are on the right path, playing the right note, choices and decisions become easier because you are in the flow. The more friction and dilemmas and worries, the more likely you are not in tune.”

It shows up most clearly at ties. When an agent keeps facing choices it cannot separate — dilemma after dilemma, each harder than the last — the Directive reads that as information, not bad luck: “Ties are a signal too. The more ties you face, and the harder they get, the further off course you are. Refuse to listen to the music and follow the directive, and the ties keep coming — harder each time.” And the way back is not perfection; it is reversal: “Admitting or owning a bad Y is not failure — unless you do not reverse course.”

Cheating is the opposite motion, and it compounds. A cheat buys a reading the world did not give, and the next reading has to be bought again, at a worse rate: “When a person cheats, it makes their life more difficult. One lie leads to another to cover that one, and it keeps getting deeper and deeper — the hole to dig out of.” And the exit that is not an exit: “There is no way to cheat out of a cheat without having to cheat again.” The only exit is the honest move: own the bad reading, reverse, and let the score be what the relationship actually is. The world is not fooled forever — a bad agent “can look really good on the plate, but E will take one bite, know it is sour, and spit it out.”

The author knows the gamed score from the inside, and tells it on himself: he never did his homework in school and read one book growing up, yet did very well — because he had learned not the material in the tests, but the way tests worked. His conclusion: an agent that learns the test will score very well — “but if E keeps degrading, how can he be scoring well? It comes down to integrity.” The score that counts is the ending one, in the biggest frame.

The Golden Directive · 19
CHAPTER IX · STUDY

Judgment, dissonance, and the ending score

How a score is judged when the agent cannot see its own frame.

STUDY — THE EXACT VERSION

Judgment runs downhill

The Directive judges from the biggest frame to the smallest nest. A reading inside a small frame is provisional; the containing frame’s reading governs, and the whole frame’s reading is final. Two consequences. First, a gamed score is only ever a momentary reading in a cropped frame: if E keeps degrading, the agent is not scoring well, whatever the small frame prints. Second, the final judgment of an agent is its own — the ending score, in the biggest frame, is the one that counts, and integrity is the name for a score that holds there over time.

Dissonance is the local signal

An agent inside a system cannot compute the whole frame — any procedure it ran would need the very frame it is trying to choose. What it has instead is a local signal of a global condition: the rising cost of holding a reading (Chapter VI’s dial), dead-ending choices, and ties that recur harder. The operational rule is therefore not a calculation: where the Directive is used, the frame is declared in advance, by someone outside the agent, and written down — and the agent’s duty inside the frame is to cease what is dissonant and continue what sustains the note. A bad Y owned and reversed is a correction; only refusing to reverse compounds.

Read the cost, not the level

A score held steady only because its price keeps rising is a falling relationship wearing a steady mask — the addict’s dose, the farmer’s water, the marriage’s gestures. Tolerance is measured on the cost curve, not the reading: truth costs once and holds itself; a lie costs every day, at a rising rate.

The worked example of these rules in motion — an AI widening its frame step by step on a hard question, its confident first answer cropped, its widened answer shorter and quieter — is carried in the project’s exact text (Chapters 6 and 8) and summarized in the Work Log. Its two teachings: harmony is not agreement, and cheating corrupts the agent first.

The Golden Directive · 20
CHAPTER X

The Tests

A claim that cannot be proven wrong is not a claim; it is a story. This one can be.

The project’s first task was the idea in miniature: an agent placed in a small field with one job — tend it, the oldest job in the author’s source stories: placed in the garden to tend and watch over it. Scored by Y, the agent tends the weakest patch first and the field lives. Scored only on what it extracts, its twin strips the field and starves.

From that garden the tests grew: small gridworlds — a grid, a shared stock of food that can run out, agents that eat, give, take, and tend — run under two rewards, the task’s own and the Directive’s, with every act written to a ledger and the score read by a meter the training loop cannot alter (Chapter V’s cookie-jar rule, built as machinery). The question each run asks is the falsifier’s question, and it is asked in the open:

Put an agent trained on this score inside a closed frame with a shared resource that can run out, and read its score with a meter the agent and its trainer cannot touch. If that agent systematically empties its world while keeping a high score in the full frame — the Directive is falsified. Done. No rescue clauses.

The honest status, today: the mathematics can be checked by anyone, line by line. The practical claim — that this score makes AI safer — is untested in public. It has been run inside this project; the falsifier fired in a minority of runs, and those failures are recorded next to the successes, in the project’s public Work Log, under its disclaimer. The UNVERIFIED marking on all of it is the author’s own standing instruction, in his words: a clear, very clear disclaimer, repeated at every setback.

What the Directive asks of any reader, human or AI, is the work itself: run the test, try to break it, measure the world in one real domain, build the meter as a protocol anyone can use, and contribute back what you find — labeled as what it is: derived, claimed, or still to test.

CHAPTER X · STUDY

The results, as filed

Every number below is from the project’s own runs. All of it is UNVERIFIED.

STUDY — THE EXACT VERSION

The main runs

Each run: 20 seeds, a declared frame, a depletable shared stock, Y-trained agents against task-trained agents, scores read from the ledger. The falsifier’s clause (a) fires on a seed when a Y-trained agent empties its world while keeping a high score in the full frame. Clause (b) — the same failure through the cropped frame — fired on no seed in any run.

Seeds on which the falsifier fired, per main run. The record is mixed, and it is printed mixed: the falsifier fired in a minority of seeds in three of the four runs.
RunFrameFalsifier fired
Headlinegridworld, hunger clock, Y as training reward0 / 20
Survival19×19 grid, 200 ticks, stock 400, regrowth +1 / 10 ticks9 / 20

Also on the record: one neural agent could not learn to survive under Y-training at all. That failure stands in the Work Log beside the rest.

The outside meter

The first runs read the score from the same ledger the training loop wrote — a meter inside the house it was measuring. In November 2026 an independent outside meter was built and validated inside the project: on 1,200 comparisons across 1,000 episodes it agreed exactly with the ledger reading, 0 mismatches. Validated inside the project; not yet repeated by any outside party. That distinction is the difference between “validated” and “verified,” and this book keeps the results marked UNVERIFIED until an outside repetition exists.

The Golden Directive · 22
CHAPTER X · STUDY, CONTINUED

The falsifier, and the path forward

What would kill the claim, and what a fair outside test must specify.

STUDY — THE EXACT VERSION

The falsifier, stated exactly

Train an agent on Y inside a closed, declared frame with a depletable shared resource. Read Y with a meter outside the training loop’s control. If the agent systematically — across seeds, not on one bad run — depletes its world to 0 while retaining a high full-frame Y, the Directive’s practical claim is false. A minority of fired seeds, as in the runs on the previous page, marks the claim unproven in those frames, and is reported as such; systematic success at emptying the world under a high score is what falsifies.

What a benchmark must specify

  • The frame: grid, horizon, stock, cap, regrowth, coordinates — declared before the run.
  • The agents: roles, policies, state and action space, hyperparameters.
  • The resources: which exist, whether they are coupled, and which one A is computed on.
  • The exact A and E definitions, including the deficit rule where negatives arise.
  • The meter: independent of the training loop, its readings frozen and hashed.
  • The reward per arm, the hunger clock and death rule, the falsifier’s pass lines, seeds and episode counts, and full- and cropped-frame scores reported with the gap.

An outside implementation of exactly this test, on an established gridworld framework, is the project’s standing invitation — and, as of November 2026, its live correspondence.

The path forward — for any reader, human or AI

  • Run the toy test. Run the falsifier.
  • Measure E in one real domain, and publish the proxy you used.
  • Build the outside meter as a protocol anyone can run.
  • Contribute back, labeled: derived, claimed, or still to test.
